about.intro: I'm Valkenburgh Margin, also known as Valk, a Computer Engineering graduate from the Polytechnic University of the Philippines. I've completed Java programming training, with experience building Java applications, PERN-stack personal projects, and client websites.
paragraphs: I'm a builder who thinks in systems. I care not just about what I build, but how I build it—planning thoughtfully, simplifying complexity, and finding efficient ways to deliver quality results.

I approach AI the same way. Beyond prompting, I continuously refine my AI development environment through custom skills, automations, and structured workflows. My goal is to make development faster and more effective without compromising quality. I review and verify the results rather than relying on AI output alone.

projects.title: AssetHub
projects.summary: A multi-tenant equipment workspace for checkout, returns, location transfers, maintenance, audits, and retained lifecycle history.
projects.roleSummary: Hand-coded original; AI-assisted interface redesign and later development, informed by user research.

gallery.caption: Asset register · A published AssetHub screenshot of the workspace inventory.

gallery.caption: Checkout form · Custodian and expected-return fields before submission; no saved checkout is shown.

gallery.caption: Workspace dashboard · Published light-theme capture with synthetic workspace data.

projects.overview: AssetHub helps equipment managers see who holds an asset, where it is, and what happened to it. Workspace permissions connect checkout, returns, maintenance, audits, and retirement with retained history.

architecture.summary: Workspace membership and role checks happen on the server before tenant-scoped records are read or changed.

accessModel.summary: Authentication identifies the user; an active membership is checked for the selected organization on protected requests. Choosing an organization alone does not grant access.

roles.name: MANAGER
roles.scope: Manages inventory, locations, categories, maintenance, and audits.

roles.name: MEMBER
roles.scope: Views workspace assets and reports issues.

workflow: Staff with inventory permissions add equipment with its location and identifying details.
A checkout records the custodian and expected return.
Returned equipment, location changes, and maintenance remain in its history.
Location audits compare a fixed snapshot and reject stale updates.
Retired assets remain recorded rather than disappearing from the workspace.

decisions.title: Scope every workspace operation
decisions.body: Organization membership is checked on server requests, and tenant-specific relationships constrain records. Reads and writes use workspace scope rather than relying on client-side filtering.

decisions.title: Protect concurrent custody changes
decisions.body: A database constraint allows only one open checkout per asset. Asset transitions and activity history are committed together. Conflicting attempts need an explicit response instead of assigning two custodians.

decisions.title: Preserve history through the lifecycle
decisions.body: Assets retire instead of being deleted. Version checks reject stale audit updates so a saved audit does not silently overwrite newer state. Retaining retired records uses storage in exchange for keeping the asset's context.

sourceEvidence.label: Organization membership middleware
sourceEvidence.detail: Resolves an active membership before protected workspace operations.

sourceEvidence.label: Tenant and lifecycle integration tests
sourceEvidence.detail: Includes cross-tenant, member-permission, concurrent-checkout, and lifecycle checks.

projects.role: I hand-coded the original. In v2 I used AI for frontend redesign and deployment. In v3 I used AI for redesign, development, and deployment, with user research informing feature selection. I review missing features, expected outputs, and behavior.

projects.title: ARCTIC
projects.summary: A client-origin service workspace connecting requests, dispatch, work orders, inventory, and billing across branches.
projects.roleSummary: Requirements, workflows, and data decisions; AI-assisted development and deployment.

gallery.alt: ARCTIC local demo dashboard with the day’s service jobs, dispatch, maintenance, inventory, and invoice summaries.
gallery.caption: Dashboard · Local seeded demo with synthetic service records · Captured October 8, 2026.

gallery.alt: ARCTIC completed work-order details, showing synthetic service information, technician assignment, job status, and billing context.
gallery.caption: Completed work-order details · Synthetic service record in the local demo · October 8, 2026.

gallery.alt: ARCTIC billing table with synthetic invoices, paid and unpaid amounts, outstanding balances, and branch labels.
gallery.caption: Invoices and payments · Synthetic collection records in the local demo · Captured October 8, 2026.

projects.overview: ARCTIC connects customer requests and technician assignment to work orders, equipment, and billing. It starts from requirements gathered from a real company. The client project did not proceed further; the portfolio implementation is complete for its current scope.

architecture.summary: The interface supports branch workflows; the API applies organization and branch checks before data access.

accessModel.summary: These are the application's two account roles. A technician is an assignee, not a third sign-in role; technician and booking must share a branch.

roles.name: BRANCH_LEADER
roles.scope: Reads and writes stay within the user's assigned branch.

workflow: Staff record service requests for a customer, site, branch, and unit.
A job is scheduled and assigned to a technician in its branch.
The work order records inspection outcomes before completion.
An invoice follows completed work; collections and receipts are recorded separately.
Managers review jobs, stock, maintenance, and balances by branch.

decisions.title: Make job progression explicit
decisions.body: A shared transition map permits the documented job states in order. Completed and cancelled jobs are terminal through the ordinary status flow, so a normal edit cannot silently reopen work. The stricter flow limits ad hoc status edits in exchange for a predictable lifecycle.

decisions.title: Enforce organization and branch boundaries
decisions.body: Server-side queries and writes check the organization, branch, and related records. The workflow does not rely on the interface alone to hide another branch’s data. This adds scope validation to each operation in exchange for enforcing the boundary on the server.

decisions.title: Keep payment history auditable
decisions.body: Amounts use fixed-precision decimal fields. Payment moves through unpaid, partial, and paid states; a refund requires its own recorded workflow rather than resetting a paid invoice. Separate records add bookkeeping but preserve how a balance changes.

sourceEvidence.label: Branch access rules
sourceEvidence.detail: Server helpers used for organization, branch, unit, customer, and technician scope.

sourceEvidence.label: Booking status tests
sourceEvidence.detail: Focused checks for the service-job lifecycle.

projects.role: I gathered requirements, defined workflows, made data-architecture decisions, and reviewed features and outputs. Development and deployment are AI-assisted.

The gallery uses synthetic local demo records.

projects.title: CASH-G
projects.summary: A banking simulator for practicing account and transfer workflows, with a Java desktop original and a separate web adaptation.
projects.roleSummary: Hand-coded desktop v1; AI-assisted redesign, development, and deployment of Web v2.
projects.statusText: Desktop v1 + Web v2 · Public source

gallery.caption: Web v2 dashboard · Local H2 demo with synthetic practice accounts · Captured October 8, 2026.

gallery.caption: Web v2 transfer review · A synthetic recipient and amount appear before confirmation · Captured October 8, 2026.

gallery.caption: Web v2 transfer receipt · Synthetic local result, with no real account or payment network · Captured October 8, 2026.

projects.overview: CASH-G lets learners practice account and transfer workflows with synthetic data. The desktop application separates interface, services, and persistence; the web adaptation adds a review step before confirming a transfer.

architecture.summary: These versions share a project history, not an interface or one deployment path.

workflow: Desktop v1 supports account registration and sign-in, cash-in, transfers, and per-user transaction history.
Web v2 presents multiple synthetic practice accounts and a review step before a transfer.
The local web demo also includes requests, fictional billers, savings goals, cards, activity, and statement export.

decisions.title: Desktop v1: keep a transfer together
decisions.body: The Java persistence layer keeps the sender debit, recipient credit, and paired ledger entries in one database transaction. Coordinated rollback adds error handling in exchange for keeping a partial transfer out of the ledger.

decisions.title: Desktop v1: represent money deliberately
decisions.body: Java monetary values use BigDecimal and database numeric columns. Decimal arithmetic requires explicit scale and rounding decisions in exchange for avoiding binary floating-point representation of money.

decisions.title: Web v2: review before confirmation
decisions.body: The web adaptation presents the recipient and amount before confirming a synthetic practice transfer. The extra review step gives the user an opportunity to catch input mistakes.

sourceEvidence.label: Java transfer service
sourceEvidence.detail: Desktop v1: input checks and the Java transfer service boundary.

sourceEvidence.label: JDBC transfer transaction
sourceEvidence.detail: Desktop v1: commits or rolls back the persisted transfer.

sourceEvidence.label: Transfer persistence test
sourceEvidence.detail: Desktop v1: checks sender debit, recipient credit, and recipient TRANSFER_RECEIVED history.

projects.role: I hand-coded desktop v1's Java interface, services, JDBC persistence, and tests. Web v2 is an AI-assisted web adaptation, including redesign, development, and deployment. I review features, outputs, and behavior.
